title: DoD Standard Internet Protocol
summary: A 1980 specification of the DoD Standard Internet Protocol, an early form of IP for moving datagrams across connected networks. It was replaced by RFC 791 and updated by RFC 777.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet Protocol carries independent datagrams from source hosts to destination hosts across connected networks. It can split a datagram for a network with a smaller packet limit, but it does not guarantee delivery or order.

subtitle: The 1980 DoD Internet Protocol specification for datagrams across connected networks.

tldr.problem: Data needed to travel from a source host to a destination across interconnected networks with different packet-size limits.
tldr.mechanism: IP carries addresses in datagram headers and supports fragmentation and reassembly. It does not provide delivery reliability, sequencing, flow control, or data retransmission.
tldr.outcome: RFC 760 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 791; it was also updated by RFC 777.

today: RFC 760 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 791. The unit metadata also lists an update by RFC 777.

sections.title: What Internet Protocol Does
sections.content:
RFC 760 specifies the DoD Standard Internet Protocol for interconnected packet-switched networks. It moves a datagram from a source to a destination identified by fixed-length addresses.

Each datagram is independent. IP does not provide reliability, flow control, sequencing, or retransmission; higher-level protocols may provide those services.
sections.plainLanguage: IP carries each datagram independently toward its destination. It does not promise that a datagram arrives, arrives once, or arrives in order.

sections.title: How a Datagram Travels
sections.content:
An Internet module in a host creates a datagram header and passes the datagram to a local network protocol. A gateway can remove the local network header, inspect the Internet address, and send the datagram through another network toward its destination.

The IP header carries source and destination addresses and a protocol field identifying the next-level protocol. The RFC describes addresses as 32 bits, made up of an 8-bit network number and a 24-bit local address.
sections.plainLanguage: A host adds an IP header, then hands the datagram to its local network for delivery to the next host or gateway. Gateways use the destination address to forward it.

sections.title: The Internet Header
sections.content:
The header identifies the version, header length, service type, total length, identification, flags, fragment offset, time to live, next protocol, header checksum, and source and destination addresses. Version 4 is described here; the minimum header length is five 32-bit words.

Total Length includes both the header and data and is represented by a 16-bit field. The checksum covers only the header and is recalculated when header fields change. Optional fields can carry functions such as source routing, return route, and timestamps.
sections.plainLanguage: The header gives routers the addresses, size, and protocol information they need to handle the datagram. Its checksum checks the header, not the data.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content:
A datagram may need fragmentation when the next network has a smaller maximum packet size. The identification field groups fragments, the fragment offset marks each fragment's position in the original datagram, and the more-fragments flag indicates whether another fragment follows.

Offsets use 8-octet units, and fragment data is divided on 8-octet boundaries. A datagram marked Don't Fragment is discarded if it cannot be delivered without fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: If a network cannot carry a whole datagram, IP can divide it into fragments. The destination uses their identifiers and offsets to put the pieces back together.
